# Edges of the map {#sec-edges}

The two questions in this book are about index structure and frame. They
deliberately say nothing about the surface the data describes. This last
chapter is about where that silence matters, and what lies past it.

## The ladder does not know about the sphere

A regular 1 degree longitude and latitude grid has 360 by 180 cells. By the
ladder it is as regular as a grid can be. But its top row is 360 cells that
all touch one point, the pole. Column 0 and column 359 are neighbours across
the antimeridian and as far apart as possible in index space. None of this
is encoded in the grid; it is knowledge the application must supply.

That is not a failure of the ladder. Regularity is a property of the
indexing, not of the surface, which is why the same ladder works on a
plane, a sphere or a torus. The longitude and latitude case simply shows
what happens when you discretise a sphere with a tool designed for a
rectangle: the grid is correct, and the mismatch is between the grid's
scope and the application's needs.

## Workarounds that stay on the ladder

Most geoscience stays on the ladder and handles the sphere by convention:

- **Tripolar ocean grids** move the singular points onto land. The topology
  lives in the coordinate arrays and the model's halo exchange, not in the
  index.
- **Polar projected grids** such as the NSIDC grids put the pole in the
  middle of a regular grid. The antimeridian becomes an ordinary line
  through the interior.
- **Choosing the frame for the problem.** A polygon that crosses the
  antimeridian is only awkward in longitude and latitude. Warp the grid to a
  frame where the region is compact, do the work there, and the problem goes
  away. The OISST example in @sec-case-oisst is the statistical version of
  the same move.

Grid arithmetic libraries such as vaster and vapour are deliberately silent
about topology. That is the right scope: sphere topology belongs in a layer
above grid indexing.

## The binned grid: the smallest step off the ladder {#sec-l3bin}

NASA's Ocean Biology Processing Group bins level 3 ocean colour data with
the *Integerized Sinusoidal Binning Scheme*, published with SeaWiFS
(Campbell, Blaisdell and Darzi 1995) and used since for CZCS, OCTS, MODIS,
VIIRS, MERIS, Aquarius and PACE. It is worth a section of its own because it
is the simplest grid that takes the sphere seriously, and because it breaks
the ladder in an instructive way.

The rules fit in a few lines:

- the globe is split into `NUMROWS` zonal rows of equal latitude height
  (an even number, so no row straddles the equator);
- each row is divided into a whole number of equal bins, proportional to the
  cosine of the row's central latitude;
- bins are numbered from 1, south to north, and west to east from the 180
  degree meridian within each row;
- each polar row ends up with exactly 3 bins.

As arithmetic:

```
latbin[row] = (row + 0.5) * 180 / NUMROWS - 90          # row = 0 .. NUMROWS - 1
numbin[row] = int(2 * NUMROWS * cos(latbin[row]) + 0.5)
basebin[row] = 1 + sum(numbin[0 .. row - 1])
row  = int((90 + lat) * NUMROWS / 180)
bin  = basebin[row] + int((lon + 180) * numbin[row] / 360)
lon  = 360 * (bin - basebin[row] + 0.5) / numbin[row] - 180
```

| NUMROWS | Bin size | Total bins | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 180 | 1 degree, about 111 km | 41,252 | Aquarius |
| 2160 | 5 minutes, about 9.28 km | 5,940,422 | SeaWiFS, OCTS |
| 4320 | 2.5 minutes, about 4.64 km | 23,761,676 | MODIS, VIIRS, MERIS, CZCS |

: Standard L3 bin resolutions, from the OBPG format page; the totals are reproduced by `scripts/make_figures.py`. {#tbl-l3bin}

![(a) A regular grid in the sinusoidal projection is equal area but over a third of its cells fall outside the Earth (the limit is 1 - 2/pi, about 36%). (b) The L3 bin scheme with 18 rows: each row has just the bins it needs. (c) Bins per row, the ragged array that NUMROWS alone determines.](figures/l3bin.png){#fig-l3bin}

**Why ragged.** The sinusoidal projection is equal area, so a regular grid in
it has equal-area cells, but the Earth occupies only the lens-shaped middle
of the rectangle (@fig-l3bin a). Forcing a sphere into that rectangle leaves
about 36% of the cells empty by construction. The binning scheme keeps the
equal-area idea and drops the rectangle: each row gets as many bins as its
latitude band needs (@fig-l3bin b). The result is a ragged array, not a
matrix.

**Where it sits on the ladder.** By the ladder's definitions this is
unstructured: there is no global (i, j) index, only a bin number. But it is
nothing like a mesh. Every bin's position follows from its number by
arithmetic, and the entire global scheme is defined by one integer,
`NUMROWS`, the way a regular grid is defined by six numbers. So L3 bins
break the usual pairing on the ladder, where implicit positions go with
structured indexing and explicit positions with unstructured. They are
implicit *and* unstructured. That combination is what discrete global grid
systems are built on, which is why the scheme reads well as the simplest
possible DGGS.

**What files store.** Because the addressing is implicit, a binned file
stores only the bins that have data: a list of bin numbers with their
statistics (observation counts, weights, sums), and a per-row index into
that list. Coordinates are never stored; they are computed from the bin
number when needed. That is the entropy argument of @sec-costumes taken to
its conclusion.

**Its limits as a DGGS.** It is the simplest, not the best:

- *Nearly* equal area. Rounding each row to a whole number of bins makes bin
  areas vary by about 7% from smallest to largest, at all three standard
  resolutions.
- Not hierarchical. Doubling `NUMROWS` does not split each bin into four;
  from 2160 to 4320 rows, only about 11% of child rows have exactly twice
  their parent's bins.
- Bins are longitude and latitude rectangles, so their shape degrades toward
  the poles, and the 180 degree meridian is still a seam.
- Neighbours in the next row are found by arithmetic on longitudes, not by a
  fixed offset.
- With 32-bit bin numbers the scheme overflows at about 41,000 rows (roughly
  500 m bins). Precision bites earlier: the OBPG page warns that 32-bit and
  64-bit arithmetic can put the same coordinates in different bins at the
  finer resolutions.
- Bins are laid out on a sphere (radius 6378.145 km), not the ellipsoid,
  which adds its own small departure from equal area.

H3, S2 and HEALPix trade more complicated addressing for hierarchy and
better cell shapes. L3 bins show what the first step away from the
rectangle looks like.

**Tools and references.** The R package hypertidy/L3bin
(github.com/hypertidy/L3bin) implements the scheme without materialising
it: `L3bin(NUMROWS)` returns the row tables, and `bin_from_lonlat()`,
`lonlat_from_bin()`, `extent_from_bin()` and `crop_bins()` work from those.

```r
library(L3bin)
L3bin(2160)$totbins                 # 5940422
bin_from_lonlat(147, -42, 2160)     # the bin containing Hobart
lonlat_from_bin(c(1, 2, 3), 2160)   # the three bins of the south polar row
```

The OBPG format page, *Integerized Sinusoidal Binning Scheme for Level 3
Data* (oceancolor.gsfc.nasa.gov/resources/docs/format/l3bins/; archived
at web.archive.org, snapshot 6 January 2026), gives the
rules, the resolution table and reference Perl routines (`initbin`,
`latlon2bin`, `bin2latlon`, `bin2bounds`); its Figure 1 uses the same 18
rows of 10-degree bins as @fig-l3bin. The original description is NASA
Technical Memorandum 104566, Volume 32. An ASCII Markdown copy of the page,
made from the archived snapshot, is kept with this project's files
(`l3bins-archive/`).

### Two things called "sinusoidal" {#sec-two-sinusoidals}

The word "sinusoidal" names two very different grids in NASA data, and
moving between them crosses the whole map of this book.

- **The ocean colour bins** above: a ragged array, unstructured but implicit,
  defined by `NUMROWS`. No CRS is needed to compute a bin's position; the
  scheme is "sinusoidal" only in the sense that row lengths follow the
  cosine of latitude.
- **The MODIS land tiles** (the "SIN grid"): a *regular* grid in a projected
  CRS, `+proj=sinu +R=6371007.181`. The world is cut into 36 by 18 tiles of
  10 degrees at the equator, 1,111,950.52 m on a side, and each tile is a
  regular raster: 2400 by 2400 cells of 463.31 m for the 500 m products,
  4800 of 231.66 m for 250 m, 1200 of 926.63 m for 1 km. Tile and cell
  positions are six numbers in that CRS, and GDAL reads them as an ordinary
  geotransform.

The second is the regular sinusoidal grid of @fig-l3bin a: equal area, and
with a large share of its cells outside the Earth, which is why tiles that
are entirely off the Earth or entirely ocean are simply not produced. In
longitude and latitude its meridians lean further from vertical with
distance from the central meridian, so a MODIS tile written out as
longitude and latitude arrays looks curvilinear, exactly like the NSIDC grid
in @fig-nsidc. And the ocean colour *mapped* products (standard mapped
images, SMI) are a third grid again: the bins interpolated onto a regular
longitude and latitude raster. At the equator an SMI pixel matches a bin
exactly; toward the poles there are more and more SMI pixels per bin, so the
regular raster repeats information the bins held once.

So the same instrument's data can arrive as a ragged equal-area index, a
regular sinusoidal raster, or a regular longitude and latitude raster, and
a reader who only hears "sinusoidal" cannot tell the first two apart. In the
two-question terms: the bins have no frame and no (i, j) index at all; the
land tiles are regular in a sinusoidal frame; the mapped images are regular
in longitude and latitude.

## Discrete global grid systems

Discrete global grid systems (H3, S2, HEALPix, ISEA) go the whole way. The
sphere comes first, and adjacency, area and hierarchy are correct by
construction. The price is the global row and column index. They sit
outside the ladder not because they are more complicated, but because they
answer a different question: what is the right cell scheme for a sphere,
rather than how is this array positioned.

## Grids as meshes {#sec-grids-as-meshes}

Every grid on the ladder is already a mesh. The (i, j) index gives the
topology for free: each cell is a quad, its corners are vertices, and its
neighbours are one step away in the index. Turning a grid into triangles
needs no triangulation algorithm at all. Split each quad in two, and the
only choice is the diagonal. That choice is real: bilinear interpolation
in a cell is linear on neither pair of triangles, and the two splits give
different values at the cell centre.

Triangulate the grid's *points* instead, and the index is thrown away. What
comes back depends on the frame the triangulation was done in, so the
title question has a mesh version: Delaunay in what? The trianglewins page
"Grids as meshes" measures it on one 10 x 10 block of the NSIDC 25 km south
grid, triangulated in longitude and latitude, in EPSG:3412 and on the
sphere (geocentric xyz):

- In its own frame and on the sphere, every triangle is half of one grid
  cell: 162 triangles for 81 cells.
- In longitude and latitude, near 60S the cells survive but 24 extra
  sliver triangles fill the block's concave edges. Around the pole only
  31% of triangles stay inside one cell; the rest fan across the
  antimeridian cut.
- Which diagonal each cell gets is a tie in EPSG:3412 and on the sphere
  alike (the corners of a square lie on a circle, and stereographic
  projection keeps circles circles), so it is decided by rounding.

The difference from grids is what can be recovered. A grid stored in the
wrong frame is still regular in its own, and the field guide can find it.
A triangulation made in the wrong frame is a different triangulation, and
no frame recovers the right one. Connectivity survives a change of frame;
straight edges, the Delaunay property, area and angle bounds, and linear
interpolation weights do not.

The word "dimension" needs care here too. The trianglewins notes separate
coordinate dimension (how many coordinates each vertex has) from
topological dimension (what kind of shape it is). In array software,
"dimension" means a third thing again: an axis. A grid with `lon(y, x)`
has two dimensions, whatever its coordinates.

## The question to carry away

Every grid in this book can be described by two short answers: how
positions follow from the index, and in which frame. Most of the grids
called curvilinear are regular in a frame someone forgot to write down.
Before you regrid, resample or reach for the 2D arrays, ask the title
question: regular in what?
